title: O(n!) — Factorial Time
description: An algorithm runs in O(n!) time when it generates or processes all possible permutations of n items. Factorial growth is even more extreme than exponential growth. While 2²⁰ is about a million, 20! is over 2 quintillion. Factorial algorithms are only feasible for extremely small inputs (n < 10-12). They typically arise when solving optimization problems by brute force or when you need to try every possible ordering of elements.
intuition: Imagine you're arranging 5 books on a shelf and want to see every possible order. The first position has 5 choices. Once you place a book there, the second position has 4 remaining choices. The third position has 3 choices, and so on. Total arrangements: 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120. That's 5! (5 factorial). With 10 books, you have 3,628,800 arrangements. With 15 books, you have over 1.3 trillion arrangements. Each new item multiplies the total by all the positions it could occupy.

examples.title: Generating All Permutations
examples.explanation: Generating all permutations of n elements produces n! different arrangements. For each of n elements, you recursively permute the remaining n-1 elements, giving n × (n-1) × (n-2) × ... × 1 = n! total permutations.

examples.title: Traveling Salesman (Brute Force)
examples.explanation: The brute-force solution to the Traveling Salesman Problem tries every possible order of visiting cities. With n cities, there are n! possible routes. This approach quickly becomes impossible: 15 cities means trying over 1.3 trillion routes.

examples.title: String Permutation Anagrams
examples.explanation: Finding all anagrams of a string means finding all permutations of its characters. A string with n unique characters has n! anagrams. The word 'code' has 24 anagrams, but 'algorithm' has over 3.6 million.

examples.title: Exhaustive Task Scheduling
examples.explanation: Finding the optimal ordering of n tasks by trying all possible orders requires evaluating n! schedules. This brute-force approach is only viable for very small numbers of tasks.

whatCausesThis:
O(n!) complexity occurs when you must generate or examine every possible ordering (permutation) of n elements. Common patterns include:

• **Generating permutations**: Any algorithm that produces all possible arrangements of n items
• **Optimization by exhaustive search**: Trying every possible order to find the optimal solution
• **Combinatorial problems**: Problems like Traveling Salesman, Hamiltonian Path, or task scheduling when solved by brute force
• **Recursive placement**: Choosing from n options, then n-1, then n-2, creating n × (n-1) × (n-2) × ... × 1 branches

The mathematical pattern: When you have n positions to fill and each position reduces the number of remaining choices by one, you get n! total possibilities.

Factorial vs Exponential:
• 10! = 3,628,800 vs 2¹⁰ = 1,024
• 15! = 1,307,674,368,000 vs 2¹⁵ = 32,768
• 20! = 2,432,902,008,176,640,000 vs 2²⁰ = 1,048,576

Factorial growth vastly outpaces even exponential growth. While exponential algorithms might work up to n=25, factorial algorithms break down around n=12.
whyItMatters:
**When It's (Extremely Rarely) Acceptable:**
O(n!) is almost never acceptable in production code. The only scenarios where it might be used:

• **n ≤ 10**: Tiny, absolutely bounded inputs (even 10! = 3.6 million operations takes noticeable time)
• **Theoretical correctness**: Academic proofs or demonstrating why better algorithms are needed
• **No better algorithm known**: Some NP-hard problems may require factorial time in worst cases

Even with n = 12, you're computing 479 million operations, which takes seconds.

**Where It's Unacceptable (Almost Everywhere):**
O(n!) is catastrophically slow for anything beyond tiny inputs:

• **n = 5**: 120 operations — instant
• **n = 10**: 3,628,800 operations — seconds
• **n = 15**: 1,307,674,368,000 operations — hours to days
• **n = 20**: 2.4 quintillion operations — years to centuries
• **n = 25**: Effectively infinite — longer than the age of the universe

Factorial algorithms are simply not feasible for real-world data. A user uploading 20 items would make your application completely unusable.

**Optimization Strategies:**
• **Dynamic programming**: Many permutation problems can be solved more efficiently by building up solutions
• **Heuristics**: Use approximate algorithms that find "good enough" solutions (genetic algorithms, simulated annealing)
• **Greedy algorithms**: Make locally optimal choices instead of exploring all possibilities
• **Branch and bound**: Eliminate entire families of permutations that can't be optimal
• **Problem reformulation**: Sometimes rephrasing the problem reveals polynomial-time solutions

The Traveling Salesman Problem, for instance, has no known polynomial-time solution, but approximation algorithms can find near-optimal solutions efficiently. In practice, you almost never implement O(n!) algorithms — you use smarter approaches.
keyTakeaways: O(n!) means generating or checking all possible orderings of n items — growth is more extreme than exponential and only viable for n < 10-12
Factorial growth: 10! is 3.6 million, 15! is over 1.3 trillion, 20! is over 2 quintillion
Permutation problems (all possible arrangements) inherently have n! possibilities
Factorial algorithms are almost never acceptable in production — always look for heuristics, approximations, or better algorithms
The Traveling Salesman Problem is a famous example where the brute-force solution is O(n!), but approximation algorithms provide practical solutions
